goals.title: Bend the island's wire
goals.critique: This is new and sits squarely on the human's direction: one material, worked by hand, with springback, work-hardening and fatigue you feel in every push, and objects that are then used and succeed or fail by their real shape. The hook that slowly opens and drops the lantern into the grass is a real clip, and reading the wire by feel is an honest skill to learn, but the pitch is a paragraph rather than one plain sentence, and a stranger cannot see from it what the mouse does at each bend. The wire friends that stand or topple, together with the friends' requests, are thin, ordinary errand scaffolding next to the strong core. The road is long: it needs 3D rod mechanics with twist on the GPU before half the promises can be tested, and the cheap first steps (hook, lantern, spring) have to prove that the feel reads at all.

goals.title: Carve a top that wins the ring
goals.critique: The loop is clear and short: cut a profile, throw, and in seconds you get a verdict that teaches you what your shape did. The dying top that knocks out its rival and then falls over is exactly the kind of last-second clip people send. But battling tops is a well-worn toy and a well-worn game genre, so the mechanic people would name the game after already belongs to others, and a lathe profile is one curve, which gives a narrow design space that may run out after a few friends are beaten. It works one material on one tool and builds nothing that stays in the world beyond a shelf, so it only touches the Minecraft-like direction, and its road mostly leads to a tournament, not to a broader island.
